leads_to.evidence: Most graduates go straight into jobs in business, finance and government. Working as an economist usually takes a master's or Ph.D., and some majors go on to law or other graduate school, so first-year pay understates them.

nearby_pair.evidence: Both are traditional undergraduate colleges in Manhattan that take freshmen straight from high school. Baruch accepts first-year applicants on a rolling basis through CUNY's standard freshman application.

school_matters.evidence: At the most selective schools, economics feeds Wall Street. Duke's economics department says about four in five majors take full-time jobs by graduation, and roughly two-thirds of those go into finance and about a sixth into consulting.

who_is_counted.evidence: Most economics degrees come from public four-year universities, and the major is taught almost entirely on campus to students who enter as freshmen. Only one program in the data is online-only.

programs.evidence: Claremont McKenna is highly selective and is one of the top liberal arts colleges for placing graduates in finance and consulting firms.
Duke's economics department reports that most of its majors take full-time jobs by graduation, mainly in finance and consulting.
Harvard is among the most selective schools in the country, and its economics graduates are recruited by top banks and consultancies.
Purchase is a SUNY campus focused on the arts with a small economics program, and nothing I found explains its low first-year pay.
New Mexico's lower wages may account for part of the gap, but I found no clear reason this program pays so far below other open-admission schools.
Fewer than twenty graduates are counted, too few for a reliable earnings figure.
